subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a custom chopper motorbike in Overwatch style, with a root frame joint and separate joints for the wheels to allow for rotation.

Sketching dimensions: roughly 2.4m long chopper with raked front fork, ape hangers, hardtail, teardrop tank, fat rear tire, and V-twin engine, oriented facing +Z with wheel axles along X. For styling, I'm going with a charcoal frame, orange tank with white stripe, teal glowing energy coils, and a custom chevron emblem instead of copying the actual Overwatch logo, while being careful to use only well-understood API helpers to avoid errors.

Now I'm working through side-view coordinates for the rear and front wheels, steering head, and fork rake angle -- placing the rear wheel center around z=-0.85 and front wheel around z=1.15 for a roughly 2.0m wheelbase, then computing the fork angle from the steering head to the front axle to land around a 40° rake.

Now I'm laying out the joint hierarchy: a root frame joint, a steer joint at the head angled along the fork direction, a front wheel joint at the axle parented to steer, and a rear wheel joint parented to the root. I'm deciding whether to add a kickstand or seat joint too.

Writing wheel geometry...

Adding wheel tread details...

Working out spoke placement...

Now I'm planning the frame geometry: a chopper hardtail built from swept tubes, with a backbone running from the steering head down to the seat post, and axle positions for front and rear wheels laid out to hit roughly a 2.6-2.7m wheelbase total length matching a real chopper.

Working out the rear fender geometry next, planning to sweep an elliptical cross-section along an arc path curving over the rear wheel.

Rather than risk getting the rotation sign wrong, I'll avoid the ambiguity entirely by computing the arc points directly with trig, writing a small helper that generates points along an angular sweep from explicit start/end angles. Then I need to figure out which axis corresponds to the box section's width for the fender sweep.

For the fender's box cross-section, since the path lives in the YZ plane, the binormal direction runs along X, so I'll set the half-width there with a thinner height, painted orange with flat caps for that chopper-style thick rear fender look.

For the gas tank, I'm weighing whether to lathe a teardrop profile around the Z axis versus loft through stations with width/height at each point, since lathing gives round cross-sections but I want flattened tank sides.

I'll go with loft, defining stations along the tank's length with varying widths and heights to taper from a narrow front near the backbone to a wide middle and tapering back toward the seat, sitting the tank slightly above the backbone at y~1.02. I still need to confirm whether loft requires a bone reference or just defaults to the nearest joint, and I'm considering a paint function for an orange base with a racing stripe pattern across the tank surface.

For the overall color scheme I'm leaning into an Overwatch-inspired palette: that bold orange, dark blue-grey, steel/gunmetal for metal parts, and cyan glow accents with white highlights, using cel shading from the toon kit for painted panels like the tank, fenders, and engine covers while keeping metallic bits on separate materials.

For the glow elements, I'll reserve the cyan for headlight lenses, tail strips, wheel inner rings, and engine coils. Now I'm working out the V-twin engine geometry — a crankcase box with two cylinders angled in a V shape, using a lathe-generated finned profile along each cylinder's axis to get that classic air-cooled look.

Writing fin profile outline...

Thinking through engine styling: dark gunmetal body with orange head covers, plus cyan glow rings at cylinder bases using lathe tori for that Overwatch tech feel. For the cylinder orientation I'll use direction vectors tilted up-forward, and the crankcase can be a simple metal-painted box.

Side covers get round lathe discs with orange caps and a cyan glow center, like a small arc reactor detail. Behind the engine I'll add a boxy transmission housing, then work out the exhaust -- planning a pair of upswept drag pipes on each side sweeping back from the cylinder heads to flared megaphone tips.

Plotting dual-header exhaust pipe curves...

Checking swingarm rail placement against tire width—rails at x=±0.1 would clip through the tire near the axle, so I need to move them outside the wheel to x=±0.15, matching the axle dropouts at ±0.14.

Now I'm designing the solo pan seat with lofted stations for a leather look, considering a dark navy color scheme with orange piping to fit the palette, and starting to think through the sissy bar shape.

Then I'm building the front fork assembly, choosing a telescopic triple-tree design over a springer, defining stanchion tubes and slider legs positioned relative to the headTop and axle points...

Writing fork and triple tree geometry...

Checking grip height against shoulder level for a chopper look, I adjust the curve points lower so bars sit around 1.2-1.34 with grips extending outward near the end, adding separate rubber grip rods with glowing caps and a thin bar radius, all attached to the steer bone.

For the mirrors, I'm adding a stalk with a small hexagonal mirror using cyan glass. Then I work out the headlight placement on the fork front, lathing a bucket-shaped shell with a glowing lens dome mounted forward along the steer direction.

I'm considering a small chevron-shaped light visor fairing above the headlight for extra detail, plus a short bobbed front fender swept over the wheel, and now I'm thinking through forward control pegs for the chopper footboards.

For the kickstand, I'm placing it stowed and folded back near the frame so its tip stays above ground level, avoiding any ground contact in the rest pose. I'm also planning the belt drive setup with a primary belt cover on the left side and a rear sprocket.

Now I'm working through positioning the rear sprocket relative to the frame rails and exhaust pipe, trying to keep enough spacing between parts so nothing overlaps -- I'm leaning toward dropping the chain detail entirely and using a simple belt guard instead to avoid the clutter of positioning a chain loop.

Planning the chain loop using a closed catmull-rom spline through six approximate points connecting the sprocket and engine gear, then sweeping it with a thin tube radius for the chain geometry.

Now I'm adding gear detail with spokes, a bore, and considering brake disc and caliper components for the wheels—a lathed ring for the disc and an orange box for the caliper. I'm also thinking through rim options, possibly using a spoked disc wheel design.

Writing wheel geometry...

Right, so the rim's half-width is smaller than the tire's cross-section, meaning it'd be completely hidden behind the sidewall. I need to widen the tire's inner radius so the rim's disc face is actually visible through the opening, designing it like a hubcap with a glowing ring detail.

Still plotting tire profile coordinates...

Checking the rim face disc geometry against the tire's inner radius — I need to verify the disc's half-thickness doesn't poke through the tire's edge width at that overlap point, especially since the front tire's width is narrower than the rear.

I'm settling on scaling the disc thickness per tire width so it sits neatly as a rim lip, adding an orange cel-shaded color plus a thin cyan glow ring near the rim edge on each face. For the disc face itself I'm skipping true spokes in favor of simple dark radial vane blocks to suggest a turbine-style wheel.

Now I'm mapping out six slender dark spokes as flat decal boxes on each wheel face (24 parts total across front/back and both wheels), then defining the hub cap, steel center, and axle rod, plus a dual brake disc ring for the front wheel while nudging the glow ring outward to avoid overlapping it.

I'm positioning the brake disc rings, checking that their radius stays within the tire's hollow bore so they're visible through the hole, then adjusting the glow ring radius and offset to clear the sidewall -- and noting the rear wheel should only get a disc on the visible right side given its larger bore.

I'll skip adding a rear disc since the sprocket occupies that side instead, keeping it just outside the rail radius with its own thickness, and adding small dropout plates at the rear axle. I'm also confirming the lathe axis orientation for the wheels so the outline profile sweeps correctly around the x-axis in local model space.

For the tire tread, I'm designing a paint function that restricts the chevron pattern to the outward-facing radial region of the tire, alternating marks every 10 degrees with an offset based on which side of the tire's axis the point falls on. I'm estimating the texel density across the painted area comes out to roughly 3mm resolution, which should be fine for 6cm-wide tread blocks.

I'll bump the paint resolution to 2048 for crispness even though it means a heavier 4096 atlas, since the body has large painted areas across most parts and I want sharp edges at the normal-based boundaries. I'm keeping the flat color palette under about 25 colors, and now sketching an original emblem decal for the tank's side — a stylized orange hex badge with a winged bolt motif instead of copying any existing franchise logo.

Now I'm working out how to apply the decal onto the tank's loft surface, mirroring it across both flanks using opposite direction vectors, and picking a surface point near the tank's taper where the width narrows — projecting the decal along the surface normal at that station. I'm deciding to skip adding any text or numbering to the decal, keeping it purely graphical.

I'm also layering in secondary details: a glowing cyan ring at the base of the cylinder fins, an orange-red "hard-light" taillight strip on the fender, and considering an underglow strip or oil-tank battery box beneath the seat, though I'm holding back from overloading the design with too many glow elements.

Now I'm thinking through a visible "power core" — a vertical glowing cyan cylinder positioned between the frame backbone and the engine, flanked by orange caps. I'm also planning a classic round air cleaner (lathe disc, orange with a glowing center) on one or both sides near the carb to nail that S&S-style intake look.

I need to double-check that the exhaust header paths from the front cylinder don't collide with the new intake geometry, but the positions seem to clear each other fine. For finishing touches, I'm adding a tank-mounted gauge — a small lathe-cup housing with a circular dial face — and I'll ditch the brass steampunk gauge texture in favor of a custom cyan-on-dark SVG HUD dial to match the bike's overall palette.

Writing SVG dial code...

Adding kickstand and rider controls like grips, then a small glowing taillight on the rear fender, shaping the fender curve path relative to the rear wheel center.

Also thinking about adding frame-mounted armor-style side plates, like a battery cover panel beneath the seat, extruded as a shaped panel in the YZ plane for visual detail.

Still checking panel clearance against seat stays...

Placing the crankcase box near the down tube's end so they coincide, then working out the lower frame rails extending from the crankcase rear back toward the axle, tracing their path coordinates as they widen from near the engine to near the rear axle.

The front down tube merges into the center, and I'm figuring out that sweep-based bone assignment can be tricky since nearby joints like the steering joint might steal segments meant for the frame rail -- I need to be careful about which joint's bone is actually closest to each path segment.

Rather than relying on proximity, I'll explicitly specify the bone for every sweep rather than letting the system infer it, which avoids ambiguity when multiple joints are near a given path. I'm defining the joint hierarchy: a root "frame" joint, with "steer" as its child, "wheelF" under steer, and "wheelR" and "kickstand" both parented to "frame" -- making sure each joint exists before any part references it.

Setting up wheelF's rotation axis to align with the fork axle so the wheel spins correctly, and deciding to skip creature-style roles like "hinge" since this isn't an articulated creature. I'm mounting the front fender and brake caliper to the steer bone so they move with the fork, then starting to write the import statements and utility helpers needed for the build.

I'm defining a color palette—orange, navy, steel, white, cyan, rubber tones—and setting up paint materials using the cel-shaded toon style for painted panels plus metal paint for engine and exhaust parts, aiming for a clean, polished look rather than a weathered one.

Now I'm writing the tank's paint logic: a function that checks position coordinates to apply orange base color with white and navy stripe bands across the top, and a darker navy cap near the front and rear ends.

For tires, I'm defining flat rubber colors for the base and tread marks, then starting to build out the chopper's structure — creating the root frame joint and working out the fork geometry using vector math to find where the front axle sits relative to the head position and fork direction.

I'm now computing the fork leg and stanchion positions using a helper function that places points along the fork direction offset by a lateral width, then adding the steering stanchions as thin steel rods, sliders as thicker gunmetal cylinders near the bottom, and planning the front axle and wheel placement with legs spaced symmetrically around the centerline.

Still working out the triple tree geometry -- placing upper and lower yoke rods, fitting the head tube between them, and figuring out where the fork tubes and handlebar risers attach.

Still writing handlebar geometry...

Adding the mirror geometry oriented toward the rider with a pale glass tint, plus an orange housing cylinder behind it, then positioning the headlight.

Working out the headlight bucket placement relative to the fork direction, computing its forward offset and mounting brackets as rods connecting the fork legs to the bucket sides, and checking that the bucket radius doesn't collide with the fork legs at their mounting height.

Shaping the lathe profile for the headlight shell and front lens dome, with a bezel ring formed by the shell lip and a separate glowing lens element protruding forward.

Writing disc paint logic...

Working out spoke positioning...

Adding brake discs and caliper geometry...

Checking where the slider sits near the bottom of the fork, I estimate the caliper position along it and settle on placing it near the slider's center, roughly matching the y and z coordinates I calculated.

I'm skipping the rear brake for now, and adding small cyan-glowing caps at the front axle nuts and fork lower ends for a nice detail touch. Now I'm moving on to the engine, starting with the crankcase position on the frame.

I'm giving the crankcase a dark gunmetal iron finish to fit a blocky Overwatch-style engine look, and setting up the two angled cylinders extending from the crank toward front and rear with finned lathe geometry and boxy heads.

Positioning orange rocker covers on top and adding glowing cyan rings around the fin bases for accent lighting.

I'm checking whether the cylinder radius exceeds the crankcase width, and noticing the two cylinder bases might actually overlap near their base given their separation and radius.

Trying wider divergence angles still leaves overlap near the base, so I'm thinking of starting the fins higher up the barrel and keeping the lower base narrow to avoid the visual collision, like real engines do.

I'm realizing the down tube path could actually intersect the front cylinder given its leaning angle, so I need to route it forward of the engine toward the cradle, keeping the cylinder's leading fin edge clear of that frame member.

Checking clearances between the rear header route, the main pipe, and the sprocket/chain guard on the left side to keep everything spaced apart by a reasonable margin, then positioning the foot pegs relative to the exhaust and front wheel so nothing overlaps with the rider's feet placement.

I'm closing the gap in the front down tube by extending it toward the crankcase, then sizing the crankcase box so it clears the ground with roughly 0.33 units of clearance, and adding a small orange bash plate underneath the engine for armor detail.

Next I'm placing the chain drive sprockets, checking that the engine and transmission sprocket positions clear the frame rails and header pipe without overlapping.

I'm closing the chain path with a sixth point behind the rear sprocket, keeping the minimum clearance positive, and setting up the sprocket thickness and chain link cross-section as small polygons. I'm placing the rear sprocket on the rear wheel bone while the chain stays attached to the frame, coloring the rear sprocket orange and the smaller one steel.
